title: The Snake Who Paid Cash (Português)

full_text:
In a quiet village lived an impoverished, hardworking farmer named Haridatta. Despite toiling from dawn till dusk under the blazing sun, his rocky fields yielded meager harvests, and his family lived on parched grain.

One sweltering noon, exhausted by labor, Haridatta lay down to rest beneath the shade of an ancient tree near his field. Looking toward a nearby termite mound, he saw a majestic, enormous black cobra emerging from a burrow, expanding its magnificent hood in the gentle breeze.

Reflecting with reverence, the farmer thought: 'Surely this serpent is the sacred guardian deity of this field! Because I have never offered him oblations, my land has remained barren!'

Hurrying to his hut, he brought a clay saucer filled with fresh, warm cow's milk and placed it respectfully before the mound, praying: 'O Lord of the Earth! Forgive my past neglect, and accept this humble offering.'

Next morning, when Haridatta returned to inspect the saucer, the milk had been drunk, and lying in the center of the clay plate was a shining, pure gold dinar!

Delighted, the farmer took the coin, purchased grain for his family, and placed another saucer of milk. Every morning without fail, the serpent drank the milk and left behind a pure gold coin. Within a year, Haridatta grew prosperous, respected, and free from want.

One season, Haridatta had to travel to a distant city for a week. He instructed his grown son: 'Every evening, place a saucer of milk before the serpent's mound, and retrieve the gold coin in the morning.'

The son placed the milk that evening and found the gold dinar at dawn. But looking at the coin, a dark, greedy thought seized the foolish youth's mind: 'This anthill must be filled with thousands of gold dinars! Why should I wait day by day for a single coin? I will kill this serpent, dig up his mound, and take all his gold at once!'

Arming himself with a heavy iron cudgel, the foolish youth walked to the mound that evening. As the cobra emerged to drink the milk, the boy struck with all his might at the serpent's head!

The blow missed the snake's skull, striking his coils. Enraged by the treacherous attack, the venomous cobra struck with lightning speed, sinking his deadly fangs deep into the youth's ankle!

The deadly venom raced through the boy's veins; he collapsed to the earth and died before he could crawl three paces.

When Haridatta returned from his journey, he found his son a corpse on the funeral pyre. Weeping bitter tears over his son's foolish greed, the farmer took a bowl of milk and walked to the mound, hoping to restore the old compact.

The cobra emerged, but remained coiled at a safe distance on the rocks: 'Haridatta! You come out of greed, while I remember the blow of your son's cudgel. The bond between us is broken forever. You cannot forget the pyre of your son, and I cannot forget my bruised coils. Depart, and return no more!'

With that, the serpent retreated into the depths of the earth, leaving Haridatta in poverty and grief.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The golden fountain flows with grace for him who takes his share;
But he who strikes with greedy hand to strip the treasure bare,
Destroys the source of all his wealth, and reaps in bitter grief
The deadly fruit that sudden haste bestows upon the thief."
moral: Greed that seeks to seize everything in a single day destroys the golden fountain of daily blessing. [PT]

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
